rv.q: Mullarkey’s latest opus proves to be that rare thing at the Royal Court, a near-unalloyed delight.

She’s flogging the family castle in Northumberland to a Russian oligarch and escaping to South Korea with a French lesbian lover. The comedy is billed as fusing Oscar Wilde and P.G. Wodehouse, and exhibits some small wit and (to begin with), the semblance of a plot.
But, for all its promise, the play doesn’t gel, too often seeming to strain for effect, and the production follows suit.
Sam Pritchard's production is heavy-handed. Watching the comic lines struggling to land is like following an actor staggering around the stage with a dagger in her chest.
But as the story progresses, it never actually seems to come across a point.

Mates in Chelsea stems from a funny concept but in the large space downstairs at the Royal Court, it feels like a satirical comedy sketch that has been overstretched to vapidity in order to fit a full length play.
Mates in Chelsea feels like a university sketch unwisely expanded.
Nothing else catches fire, though — certainly not this babyish script, which should have gone in the recycling bin before it got near a paying audience.
I’d rather watch the complete works of Jeremy Kyle than sit through this again.
What is left shining in the rubble of the Viscount’s fortune is an exceptionally well-written, exceptionally well-acted, riotous comedy of manners.
I was won over by Amy Booth-Steel’s delightful Mrs Hanratty.
But, as artistic director Vicky Featherstone’s farewell to the Court, this is a disappointment.
This is an amusing little playlet buried in 150 minutes of rhetoric.
It’s a decidedly mild time, though it passes pleasantly enough in the assured company of this cast.
Mullarkey's script is meandering, unfunny and full of unfinished ideas.
Sam Pritchard’s production feels pacey and energetic, and although it sometimes struggles to pull together all of it’s narrative threads there’s more than enough here to make it an enjoyable evening.
Rory Mullarkey’s limp satire on the landowning, moneyed upper classes pimping their ancient homes to Russian Oligarchs just feels a bit desperate.

cn.t: Mullarkey's upper-class satire divides critics sharply: some find it riotously funny with strong performances from Kynaston, but most dismiss it as toothless, grating, and a pale imitation of Wodehouse and Wilde that wastes its satirical potential.
